This manuscript presents LCTfound, a diffusion-pretrained, cross-attention U-Net foundation model for lung CT trained on a very large multi-center dataset (LungCT-28M: 105,184 scans; “more than 28 million images” in the Abstract; “more than 20 million images” in Methods), and evaluated across eight tasks from clinical diagnosis/prognosis to pixel-level image enhancement. The breadth of downstream validations is notable: mediastinal neoplasm segmentation, PAP diagnosis, NSCLC prognostication and neoadjuvant MPR prediction, whole-lung 3D modeling for navigation, virtual CTA from non-contrast CT, sparse-view reconstruction, and low-dose CT enhancement. Across tasks, LCTfound generally outperforms strong pretraining baselines (e.g., MAE, MedSAM, RadImageNet), often with few-shot fine-tuning, with clear numeric gains reported (e.g., NSCLC AUC 0.704 on LUNG1 in Fig. 2; mediastinal neoplasm internal Dice 0.7895 in Fig. 3b; consistent improvements in pixel-level metrics in Fig. 5c-d and Supplementary Fig. 23). Pretraining with a DDPM and conditioning on basic clinical metadata (window width/level, etc.; “we employed a U-net architecture enhanced by the integration of transformer blocks,” Supplementary Fig. 1; “paired clinical information…after Bert encoding” in Curation of LungCT-28M and rationale of LCTfound) is technically sound and helps explain strong few-shot performance in both semantic and pixel-level tasks.

Several aspects strengthen the work. First, the scale and curation of LungCT-28M are impressive (“five medical centers across China,” 14 disease categories selected with an NLP classifier at confidence >0.9; Data cleaning of LungCT-28M). Second, the authors assess both high-level clinical endpoints (e.g., NSCLC survival, MPR) and low-level imaging tasks, showing that diffusion pretraining confers advantages for denoising/reconstruction (“pre-training eradicated the artifacts,” Fig. 5d; “cold diffusion” for low-dose enhancement, Supplementary Fig. 3b). Third, they provide ablations of linear vs full fine-tuning for prognosis (Fig. 2a–h), Grad-CAM visualizations (Supplementary Fig. 5, 10, 13) and deployment of full-lung 3D segmentation as a cloud demo (Fig. 4d and provided URL), underscoring translational potential.

At the same time, there are important issues that need to be addressed to solidify validity, transparency, and clinical credibility.

1) Human subjects ethics, data governance, and reporting standards
- The manuscript compiles multi-center, retrospective human imaging data, including minors (“age from 1 to 84 years,” Mediastinal neoplasms section) but does not state IRB/ethics committee approvals, consent/waiver, or data-sharing governance. Please add explicit ethics statements for each participating center, approval identifiers, consent procedures (including minors), and de-identification methods, in line with Nature Portfolio human research policies.
- For datasets involving rare diseases and multi-center cohorts (mediastinal neoplasms; MPR prediction), clarify data-use agreements and whether external test data remained on-site or were centrally transferred.

2) Dataset curation, leakage control, and generalizability
- Explicitly confirm that all downstream training/validation/test cohorts are patient-disjoint from the pretraining LungCT-28M and from each other, and that no site/time leakage occurs. This is particularly important where the pretraining NLP categories include diseases overlapping with downstream tasks (e.g., “Mediastinal mass (MM), 1,444 scans,” Fig. 1b).
- The counts for LungCT-28M images are inconsistent: Abstract says “more than 28 million images,” Methods state “more than 20 million images,” and Discussion mentions “over 100 million lung CT images” in the initial pool. Please reconcile and standardize these figures, and correct the stray term “ChestCT-100K” in the Discussion (line ~475), which is not defined elsewhere.
- For PAP diagnosis, specify that patients/sessions in training and testing are disjoint (“Guangzhou First People's Hospital,” PAP section) and clarify whether negatives in training/testing are from the same hospital/timeframe.
- Report scanner vendors, models, acquisition parameters, reconstruction kernels, and dose ranges for all datasets, and analyze domain shift (e.g., center/scanner/dose) and subgroup performance (e.g., sex/age) where feasible. The initial cohort provides sex composition (276,755 males and 209,130 females; Curation of LungCT-28M), but no disaggregated performance is reported.

3) Metrics, statistical rigor, and clinical evaluation
- Segmentation: The mediastinal neoplasm study reports Dice and external validation (Fig. 3b), but without confidence intervals or statistical tests. Please add CIs and significance testing across models, and lesion-level detection sensitivity if relevant. For whole-lung 3D modeling, reporting AUROC for segmentation is unusual; include standard overlap and boundary metrics (e.g., Dice/IoU, HD95, ASSD) across the 21 structures (Fig. 4b–d). Provide error bars and define them in figure legends.
- Classification/prognosis: For NSCLC survival on LUNG1 (Fig. 2), detail the thresholding strategy for KM stratification, provide hazard ratios with CIs from Cox models, and clarify whether multivariable analyses adjusted for known confounders (stage, histology, treatment). For MPR prediction, include CIs and calibration analyses; indicate how class imbalance was handled.
- Pixel-level tasks: For virtual CTA (Fig. 5c), the text appears internally inconsistent (“VIF…0.8600” as positive vs later “VIF…0.0831” labeled among negatively correlated metrics). Please correct the metric labels and ensure all metrics are defined in Methods. Augment quantitative image metrics with a radiologist reader study on vessel conspicuity, stenosis detection, or aneurysm/dissection depiction to establish clinical plausibility, and consider vessel segmentation overlap metrics.
- Sparse-view reconstruction uses only 9 training scans and a single test scan (561 images; Sparse view reconstruction section). Conclusions should be tempered; expand testing to multiple patients and report patient-level statistics. Clarify that CIs currently reflect slice-level variability, not subject-level generalization.
- Low-dose enhancement on Mayo 2016 uses 1 training and 9 test scans at “5% dose” (Methods). Beyond PSNR/SSIM/VIF/etc. (Supplementary Fig. 23), add HU fidelity analyses in ROIs (air, soft tissue, bone) and task-based assessments (e.g., nodule conspicuity or radiomics stability) to support clinical relevance.

4) Model design and ablations
- The architecture conditions on “paired clinical information” and time embeddings. Provide ablations quantifying the contribution of metadata conditioning (window width/level, disease tags) and multi-time-step features (“four different time steps,” Fine-tuning LCTfound) to downstream performance.
- Given the breadth of claims, include a consolidated comparison table summarizing improvements across all tasks to contextualize the stated “average 7.5% improvement” and “maximum 20% increase” (Introduction; Fig. 1d), and specify whether these are absolute or relative gains.
- Report inference time and computational footprint for downstream tasks, especially the clinically salient ones (full-lung 3D segmentation and mediastinal neoplasm segmentation), building on the limitation acknowledged about speed (Discussion).

5) Clarity, consistency, and reproducibility
- Ensure metric nomenclature is consistent (e.g., AUROC vs AUC), define all error bars in figure legends, and add missing definitions for segmentation metrics in Methods (currently focused on survival and pixel-level metrics).
- The mediastinal neoplasm section alternately refers to “four external medical centers” and “five external datasets” (Fig. 3a). Please reconcile this discrepancy and provide per-center counts (Supplementary Data Table 1 is referenced).
- Code availability is appreciated. Indicate whether pretrained weights and task-specific fine-tuned checkpoints will be released. For the NLP filtering pipeline used to curate LungCT-28M, provide model details and performance on held-out annotated reports.
- In Fig. 4, an access-token bearing URL is shared for the deployed demo. Please confirm that all content is de-identified and that sharing such tokens complies with institutional policies; consider removing static tokens from the paper.

6) Imaging and presentation standards
- In Methods, specify acquisition equipment and key settings for critical tasks (microscope-equivalent items here are scanner type, detector, reconstruction kernel, slice thickness, voxel size). Where images are displayed, clarify windowing, normalization, and any channel-wise adjustments, ensuring equal processing between methods in line with best practices outlined in community image standards.

Overall, the manuscript demonstrates a compelling advance: a single diffusion-pretrained foundation model that usefully spans high-level clinical tasks and low-level reconstruction/enhancement in lung CT. The multi-task breadth, few-shot competitiveness, and strong pixel-level performance are particularly noteworthy, as evidenced in Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 23. Addressing the ethical approvals, ensuring stricter statistical reporting and patient-level validation (notably for sparse-view reconstruction and low-dose enhancement), harmonizing dataset counts and metrics, and adding clinically grounded evaluations for virtual CTA and segmentation will substantially strengthen the paper’s rigor and translational impact.

My expertise covers medical imaging, machine learning for image analysis, and clinical AI evaluation; I did not independently verify the training code, and I did not assess the security/compliance of the provided web demo.

This manuscript presents scGALA, a graph link-prediction framework for cell alignment that underpins a broad set of single-cell integration tasks. The key message is a shift from geometry-based matching to relational inference: scGALA builds intra- and inter-dataset graphs, trains a multi-head GAT in a self-supervised masked link-prediction/VGAE scheme, and refines cross-dataset matches via a score-based search that generalizes Gale–Shapley to controlled many-to-many alignments. On diverse applications—batch correction, label transfer, multiomics integration, spatial alignment, multiplet-omics unification, cross-modality generation, and spatial imputation—the method reports consistent gains, often sizable, across standard metrics (e.g., ARI, NMI, ASW, graph connectivity, FOSCTTM), with detailed benchmarking in Fig. 2–6 and ablations/robustness in Supplementary Figures (e.g., S14–S16).

The approach is technically sound and thoughtfully engineered. The graph construction is clear and modular (“Graph Construction”), combining KNN within datasets and MNN/CCA anchors across datasets (Eq. 1), with optional spatial KNN when coordinates are available. The encoder-decoder is well-motivated (“scGALA Architecture”), employing multi-head attention, a VGAE latent space with inner-product edge decoder, feature reconstruction for representation quality, and a triplet loss when spatial edges exist (Eq. 5). The score-based search introduces a principled way to avoid over-alignment through a quadratic penalty (Eq. 6–8). The breadth of downstream demonstrations is a major strength: as a plug-in booster, scGALA consistently improves established tools (Fig. 3); as a standalone engine, it enables non-trivial capabilities such as multiplet-omics integration from disjoint doublet datasets (Fig. 4), RNA-from-ATAC generation with preserved biology (Fig. 5), and spatial gene imputation with maintained domain structure (Fig. 6).

Strengths
1. Conceptual advance: reframing alignment as link prediction with self-supervised edge masking (“Overview of scGALA”; Fig. 1a) and a principled post-hoc optimization that balances alignment coverage and specificity (Eq. 6–8).
2. Versatility and plug-and-play design: seamless replacement of alignment modules in Seurat, INSCT, scCross, scGCN, Conos, STAligner, GCN-SC (“All-in-one Integration and Harmonization Pipeline”; “scGALA as Universal Booster”), with consistent performance gains (e.g., batch correction ARI/NMI improvements in Fig. 2b and Fig. 3b; FOSCTTM reductions in Fig. 2f and Fig. 3f).
3. Robustness analyses: demonstrated tolerance to noisy/sparse anchors (Supplementary Fig. S14), ablations supporting design choices (GAT over GCN, thresholding versus score-based search, use of spatial edges; S15a–c).
4. Advanced applications with concrete gains: (i) multiplet-omics alignment with stronger diagonal signal in confusion matrices and higher AUROC (Fig. 4b,e); (ii) cross-modality generation preserving markers, clustering, pathways, and intercellular signaling (Pearson 0.93 on marker means; Fig. 5a–d); (iii) spatial imputation improving GraphST ARI (0.51 vs. 0.47) and pathway detection (Fig. 6b,d).
5. Reproducibility intent: a public code repository is provided (“Software Availability”).

There are, however, places where the evidence and presentation could be strengthened to meet the standards of a general-interest journal.

1) Statistical rigor and reporting
- Most comparisons use one-sided Student’s t-tests (e.g., Fig. 2f, Fig. 3h). Please justify the one-sided alternative a priori and report whether distributions and pairing justify parametric tests. Given repeated evaluations across many metrics and methods, control for multiple comparisons or report adjusted P-values. Where metrics are computed across repeated subsamples/splits, clarify the unit of replication, the number of repeats, and variance sources. Provide effect sizes alongside P-values.
- For alignment evaluation, ROC/AUROC is shown (Fig. 4e) but alignment positives are typically sparse; precision–recall (PR) curves and average precision would be more informative. Please include PR analyses and calibration plots for predicted link probabilities (e.g., reliability diagrams) to assess decision thresholds used by the score-based search.

2) Scope and generalization
- Many demonstrations focus on a few datasets (e.g., Mouse brain multiome + Visium in Fig. 2; PBMC multiome and large CITE-seq for Fig. 4–5; human DLPFC for Fig. 3g–h; breast cancer FFPE for label transfer in Fig. 3c–d). To substantiate generality, summarize performance across additional tissues/conditions or provide a table with all datasets used, sizes, modalities, and per-dataset metrics, including Supplementary figures referenced (S1–S13).
- For cross-modality generation (Fig. 5), results are compelling within one PBMC dataset. Please add train/test splits that enforce donor/study separation to establish out-of-domain generalization, and report per-gene and per-cell correlation distributions (not only marker means). Include error analyses on rare types and along continuous trajectories.

3) Benchmarking details and ablations
- Hyperparameters: “randomly mask 30% links” is stated in Fig. 1a, while Eq. 5 uses Bernoulli(γ) but γ is unspecified. Please reconcile and report γ, number of attention heads N_h, latent dimension d_z, K for KNN/MNN, learning-rate schedules, early-stopping criteria, and seeds for all runs. For the score-based search, specify λ selection and sensitivity.
- Graph construction uses unweighted unions (Eq. 1). Consider and report whether weighting KNN vs. MNN vs. spatial edges alters performance; an ablation with weighted adjacency or edge-type dropout would clarify robustness to edge composition.
- The spatial triplet loss (Eq. 5) depends on negative sampling from non-adjacent cells; detail the sampling strategy and show sensitivity to margin α and to spatial neighborhood size.
- Provide runtime/memory profiles, especially for large graphs (e.g., 47,681 Visium spots in Fig. 3g) and for the spatial imputation module using ClusterGCN (Eq. 12). Reporting wall-clock times and peak memory on standard hardware would help users choose settings.

4) Evaluation design and potential confounders
- Spatial imputation (Fig. 6): the ARI gain from 0.47 to 0.51 is positive but modest. Please add statistical testing across multiple spatial sections or bootstraps of spot subsets, and report fidelity on measured “held-out” genes (e.g., masked-at-random control) to further rule out overfitting to common-gene structure. Clarify whether the snRNA-seq reference and spatial data come from matched individuals and how hemispheric differences (stated in “scGALA Enables All-in-one…”) might bias imputation.
- Multiplet-omics integration (Fig. 4): beyond confusion matrices and AUROC, report recall/F1 and per-type coverage of “scGALA-exclusive” links to quantify the coverage–precision trade-off. The NEAT-seq simulation control (Supplementary Fig. S8) is useful; please add PR curves and show how performance scales with increasing noise/dropout.
- Batch correction and modality mixing often trade off. In Fig. 3b, some batch metrics slightly decline; a short analysis of when/why scGALA prioritizes biological conservation over mixing would aid users.

5) Clarity, notation, and reproducibility
- Several equations contain notation artifacts that impede reproducibility (e.g., “/latticetop”, “/epsilon1”, “∨” used for union without definition until Eq. 1). Please proofread the math, standardize symbols, and explicitly define all variables and matrix operations (attention vectors, decoder definitions, normalization). Ensure all shapes are consistent and provide pseudo-code for the score-based search.
- In “All-in-one Integration…”, clearly state how scGALA’s ˆA is injected into each baseline (e.g., Seurat’s CCAIntegration, FindTransferAnchors), and whether dimensionality reduction/UMAP/clustering use identical configurations after substitution.
- To facilitate reuse, pin the GitHub commit, provide conda/environment files, all scripts for reproducing Fig. 2–6, and deposit alignment matrices/probabilities (A′) for benchmark datasets. For stochastic components, list seeds and number of repeats.

6) Human data ethics and data provenance
- The study reuses human datasets (e.g., a 4-patient breast cancer FFPE cohort in Fig. 3c–d; PBMC donors; DLPFC spatial slices). Please add a brief statement clarifying data sources, accession links, and that reuse complied with the original consent and data-use terms, consistent with the “Research with human participants” guidance.

Minor points
1. In “Discussion,” the claim of “Spearman correlation > 0.85 to ground truth” for spatial imputation would benefit from a pointer to the exact figure/analysis (Fig. 6 reports ARI, GOBP, marker correlations).
2. In “Methods: Data Preprocessing,” justify the fixed choice of 2,000 HVGs and report sensitivity (Supplementary Fig. S10–S13 begin to address this; a concise summary in the main text would help).
3. Define precisely how FOSCTTM was computed (sample sizes, matching strategy) in Fig. 2f and Fig. 3f.
4. For Fig. 5b, ARI values are nearly identical (0.68 vs. 0.67); include trustworthiness/continuity or kNN-overlap to complement clustering-based concordance.

This manuscript introduces a multi-agent Q-learning framework to search large strategy spaces in repeated games and reports the emergence of a simple, memory-two bilateral reciprocity (MTBR) strategy. By extracting decision rules from the learned Q-tables, the authors describe MTBR as (i) forgiving a partner’s initial defection if it itself cooperated in round 1, (ii) attempting to break two-step mutual defection by cooperating once, and (iii) otherwise mirroring the opponent’s last move (“Memory-two bilateral reciprocity strategy”). Across pairwise tournaments (Fig. 3), imitation dynamics in evolving populations (Eq. 4; Fig. 4), and diverse payoff structures and network topologies (Fig. 5), MTBR attains high payoffs and frequently rises to dominance, while also improving population-wide welfare. The approach is clearly laid out (Fig. 1; “Multiagent Q-Learning framework”, “Training Process”, “Pseudocode”), making the conceptual contribution accessible.

I view the primary contribution as methodological and conceptual: using MARL to reveal a compact, interpretable memory-two policy that generalizes well beyond its training environment. The empirical findings are compelling: rapid establishment of cooperation in head-to-head play relative to TFT and GradualTFT (Fig. 2), improved average payoffs at the population level upon MTBR’s introduction in both strategy sets (Fig. 3), dominance and higher global welfare in evolving well-mixed populations across selection intensities (Fig. 4e–f), and broad efficacy across PD/SH/HG and network structures with a well-defined boundary of challenge in SG near 2R = T + S (“The dominance of MTBR in various games and networks”; Fig. 5). The addition of analytical replicator predictions (Eq. 13; Fig. 4c) strengthens the story.

Strengths
1. A general, scalable MARL framework with explicit memory-length control and transparent Q-table representation (“Multiagent Q-Learning framework”, “Pseudocode”).
2. Discovery of a simple, interpretable policy (MTBR) whose rules are succinctly summarized and mechanistically sensible in PD (forgiveness and deadlock breaking; “Memory-two bilateral reciprocity strategy”; Fig. 2).
3. Thorough evaluations: pairwise payoffs (Fig. 3), evolving populations with Fermi imitation (Eq. 4; Fig. 4), sensitivity to selection intensity (Fig. 4d–f), cross-game and network robustness (Fig. 5).
4. Integration of analytical dynamics (replicator equations, Eq. 13) that qualitatively match simulations (Fig. 4c), adding credibility.

Weaknesses and points needing clarification
1. Training–evaluation mismatch and potential bias. The training PD uses R = 2, S = 0, T = 3, P = 0.1 (“Training Environment”), which makes DD especially unattractive, and θ = 0.8 prioritizes payoff maximization in the win/loss-augmented reward (Eq. 2). It is unclear whether MTBR robustly emerges under more standard or harsher training regimes (e.g., R = 3, S = 0, T = 5, P = 1), or under different θ. The current choice may predispose agents toward cooperative and forgiving behaviors.
2. Limited ablations on the learning rule. The reward shaping in Eq. (2) depends on ex post average-payoff comparison and blends per-round and per-episode incentives. Its role in producing MTBR is not disentangled (no θ sweep, no comparison to standard Q-learning without the “win/loss” gate). Likewise, ε, Itotal, Q-initialization, and any ε annealing are not specified in the main text; these choices can strongly affect convergence.
3. Strategy pool dependence. Agents were trained against a fixed mentor set (“Mentor strategies”) and then compared to the same or related sets (Fig. 3). Robustness to mentor composition and to out-of-distribution opponents is not fully assessed. The zero-determinant subset in set 2 is mentioned but not parameterized in the main text (labels such as ZDGTFT2, ZDGen2 appear in Fig. 3b); precise definitions should be provided and referenced in Methods.
4. Formal specification of MTBR. The verbal summary is helpful, but a complete policy table for all two-step states (probabilities of C/D) is not provided. Without the exact mapping from all states to actions, replication and independent analysis are hindered.
5. Statistical reporting. Figures show averages (e.g., “averaged over 10,000 repeated experiments” in Fig. 3), but error bars, confidence intervals, or variance measures are largely absent. In Fig. 4c, dashed trajectories from 50 repeats are overplotted, but quantitative uncertainty is not summarized.
6. Notational clarity. Several equations and symbols are garbled by typesetting (e.g., Nstate in “Multiagent Q-Learning framework”, /lscript, /epsilon1, “/negationslash”). The formula for Nstate appears malformed and should be restated cleanly (and verified against Supplementary Note 1).
7. Network-evolution implementation details. For Fig. 5c–d, update scheduling (synchronous/asynchronous), interaction neighborhoods, network size, initial composition, stopping criteria, and boundary conditions (for the lattice) are not fully specified in the main text.
8. Noise robustness. Results emphasize noiseless play (“It is noteworthy that in a noiseless repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma,” near Fig. 2). Many classic insights hinge on trembles. There is no assessment of action/observation error and its impact on MTBR’s stability and abundance.
9. Claims of “dominance.” The manuscript appropriately nuances MTBR’s weakness along 2R = T + S in SG (Fig. 5 and related text). Elsewhere, “dominance” should be precisely defined (e.g., abundance at evolutionary equilibrium under Eq. 4 for a specified δ-range; or average-payoff superiority across a specified opponent set), and claims aligned to those definitions.

Suggestions to strengthen the manuscript within scope
1. Provide full MTBR specification: a complete memory-two policy table with action probabilities for all states; and release the learned Q-table(s) used to derive the rule.
2. Add ablations on the learning parameters: at minimum, a θ sweep for Eq. (2), plus results for training under the standard PD matrix R = 3, S = 0, T = 5, P = 1; report whether MTBR (or a close variant) still emerges. Include Itotal, ε (and whether it is annealed), Q-initialization, and sensitivity to α and γ.
3. Expand mentor and evaluation robustness: (i) vary the mentor pool composition during training; (ii) evaluate against additional unseen strategy mixes; (iii) report whether MTBR maintains its advantages. In Methods, fully define and reference all ZD strategies used in set 2.
4. Report uncertainty throughout: add error bars or shaded confidence intervals to bar plots and trajectories (define error metrics in legends), and provide the numerical payoff matrices underlying Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 in Supplementary Data or Source Data.
5. Clarify notation and formulas: correct the expression for Nstate and remove typesetting artifacts (/epsilon1, /lscript, “/negationslash”); restate all symbols in Eq. (2)–(4) and (13) unambiguously.
6. Specify network-evolution protocols for Fig. 5: network sizes, update rules (local Fermi along edges vs. global sampling), synchronous/asynchronous updates, initial conditions, number of generations, and convergence criteria.
7. Assess noise robustness: introduce low-probability trembles in action execution and, if feasible, perception errors; report MTBR’s pairwise payoffs and evolutionary abundance under noise.
8. Theoretical insight on SG boundary: formalize the condition 2R > T + S for MTBR advantage (already argued in text around Fig. 5) with a short analysis comparing stationary payoffs of mutual cooperation vs. alternation against key opponents (e.g., TFT), even in a simplified memory-one setting; this would sharpen the interpretive boundary.
9. Data and code availability: provide code, random seeds, and configuration files for training, tournaments, and evolutionary simulations, along with raw Q-tables and source data for figures.

Clarity and context are generally good. The Introduction situates the work well within repeated game strategy design and the limitations of memory-one analyses, and the Results articulate where MTBR excels and where it does not (Fig. 5). The Methods describe the imitation dynamics and replicate the continuous-time approximation (Eq. 13) coherently. Addressing the above points—especially full policy disclosure, training ablations, mentor/evaluation robustness, noise tests, and notational cleanup—would substantially increase confidence in the generality and reproducibility of the conclusions.

Expertise and limits: I am comfortable evaluating evolutionary game theory, repeated games, and reinforcement learning at the level presented. I did not assess any code (none provided) and could not verify the exact parameterizations of the zero-determinant strategies beyond what is implied by Fig. 3b labels.

This manuscript argues convincingly that a simple morphological trait—cell aspect ratio—can determine competitive outcomes during bacterial range expansion. Using three non-motile E. coli substrains with different shapes (Table 1; Fig. 1A), the authors show that longer cells consistently take over the expanding front in 2D colonies, even from extreme initial minority, and that the mechanism is mechanical: emergent local nematic alignment forms “channels” that deliver longer cells to the front, where they align with the interface and exclude shorter neighbors (Fig. 2A–D). A minimal agent-based model with only aspect ratio differences recapitulates the phenomenon, and a continuum bi-phasic active nematic model reproduces the same channeling and front-takeover dynamics. The advantage persists, although reduced, in 3D growth initiated from micro-beads (Fig. 4). The integration of experiments with two levels of modeling makes a strong case for a generic, alignment-driven takeover mechanism.

The key experimental observation is robust sector takeover by the longer strain across inoculation ratios, including ξ = 0.001 (“one in thousands”), with azimuthal spread and curvature of long-cell sectors around shorter-cell sectors at larger radii (Fig. 1B–C: “WT always wins over AK, even when initially outnumbered by as much as ξ = 0.001”). Time-lapse microscopy at single-cell resolution shows that long WT cells align radially in the colony interior and tangentially at the front (Fig. 2C–D), concomitant with a rising local nematic order parameter for WT relative to AK over time (Fig. 2E). The agent-based simulations replicate these spatio-temporal alignment patterns and the emergent channeling-to-front (Fig. 2A–B), and the continuum model shows activity-driven phase segregation without invoking free-energy phase separation. Takeover rates, quantified as the slope of S(r) near S ≈ 0, scale with the difference in aspect ratios and depend critically on whether the shorter strain is itself nematically ordered (Fig. 3A–D). In 3D, the longer strain still occupies disproportionate surface area relative to its initial fraction in the inoculation bead, but the strength is weaker (Fig. 4B–C).

The overall narrative is coherent and the evidence largely supports the conclusions. I see particular strengths in: (1) the elegant, minimal mechanistic modeling (fixed width, equal growth, repulsive rods) that isolates aspect ratio as the sole difference yet reproduces all salient phenomena; (2) the single-cell alignment measurements that mirror model predictions (PDF(θ) in Fig. 2D; increasing nematic order for WT in Fig. 2E with “p < 0.001” at later times); and (3) the careful quantification of competition outcomes via S(r) and takeover rates v, with replication numbers reported (Fig. 3A–B).

There are, however, a few important issues that should be addressed to solidify the causal attribution to aspect ratio per se and to strengthen quantitative claims.

Major points that require attention
1. Decoupling aspect ratio from width/volume. Table 1 shows that strains differ in both length and width (WT: 0.68 µm; AS: 0.99 µm; AK: 1.05 µm), hence also in volume. Although the agent-based model fixes width and isolates length, the experiments do not. The statement that “WT outcompetes AK even for low ξ … this slight advantage (in numbers) of WT is not enough” is helpful but not sufficient to exclude effects of width-dependent friction/adhesion or local packing. Two feasible controls would substantially strengthen causality:
   - 1) Within-genotype modulation of length at near-constant width/physiology (e.g., transient FtsI inhibition to elongate WT; brief cephalexin pulses producing modest lengthening rather than filamentation). A demonstration that a lengthened WT outcompetes its untreated sibling would be compelling.
   - 2) Competitions normalized by CFUs for 2D spots (as done for 3D, Fig. 4B–C) to remove OD-to-cell-number ambiguities; report CFU-normalized ξ and show the ξ-dependence of S(r) (Fig. 1C) under this normalization.

2. Potential confounding by mreB pleiotropy. mreB mutations can alter cell wall architecture and surface interactions, not just shape. The purely mechanical explanation is attractive, but differences in adhesion/friction could also produce differential access to fronts. At minimum:
   - 3) Provide a control showing similar monoculture front speeds for WT, AS, and AK on 1.5% agar (under the same imaging conditions), or front speeds normalized to single-cell growth rates (Supplementary Fig. S2 reports similar growth rates, but in liquid vs agar growth can diverge).
   - 4) Assess robustness to substrate mechanics by repeating a subset of 2D competitions on a second agar concentration (e.g., 1.0% or 2.0%). If alignment-driven takeover is the core mechanism, qualitative outcomes should persist.

3. Fluorescent marker and plasmid load controls. The text notes “no systematic dependence on the colour (Supplementary Fig. S5)”. Please quantify this explicitly:
   - 5) Swap fluorophores for each pair and report S(r) and v with confidence intervals. Confirm matched promoter/copy number and comparable expression burdens, or include a no-fluorescence control competition assessed by post hoc plating to rule out metabolic-load biases.

4. Statistical and analytical clarity. A few definitions and choices need tightening:
   - 6) Define precisely the statistical test used in Fig. 2E (the text implies a two-sample test on distributions; specify test, sample size N cells, and whether frames/colonies were treated as independent). Clarify error bars throughout (e.g., Fig. 2B–D PDFs: show bootstrap CIs if possible; Fig. 3A–D already report ±SEM and n).
   - 7) For v (Fig. 3B,D), report the exact fitting window around S ≈ 0 and demonstrate that v is insensitive to modest changes in that window. In simulations (Fig. 3C–D), include a short sensitivity analysis showing that takeover persists across a range of growth noise and interaction strengths.
   - 8) For 3D, S3(t2) is evaluated at t2 = 10 h. Provide a brief time series for one condition to show that the trend is not transiently reversed at later times, or justify why 10 h is representative of the range-expansion regime.

5. Imaging and processing transparency. The figures are maximum-intensity projections and pseudo-coloured composites (Fig. 1B, Fig. 2C, Fig. 4A). In line with community standards:
   - 9) State in the Methods and figure legends that any brightness/contrast adjustments were linear and applied equally to channels and conditions; disclose any gamma changes or per-channel adjustments for merged images.
   - 10) Share the raw time-lapse stacks and the segmentation/analysis code used to compute orientation, PDFs of θ, S(r), and local nematic order. For orientation analysis, specify window sizes, neighbor definitions (“8 closest neighbours”), and front-detection algorithm.

Additional constructive suggestions
1. Coffee-ring effects (Fig. 1B). Because the “coffee ring” sets an early compositional inhomogeneity, consider adding a control that minimizes ring formation (e.g., surfactant, humidity control, or gentle spin-coating) to show the mechanism is not seeded by initial edge enrichment.

2. Model–experiment parameter mapping. The simulation uses lL = 8 and lS spanning isotropic–nematic transition at lS ≈ 3.25 (Fig. 3D). It would help to provide a qualitative mapping to the experimental lengths in Table 1, clarifying that absolute values differ but the isotropic–nematic crossover is the relevant control parameter. A short note on robustness to aspect-ratio polydispersity would be valuable.

3. Continuum model details. The “bi-phasic active nematic” result is an important generalization. Please add a brief parameter table in the SI and show that takeover persists across a range of activity and elastic contrast ratios, to avoid the impression that the outcome requires fine-tuning.

4. Context and prior work. The manuscript already cites sectoring and layering literature (e.g., “sector boundaries (38, 39) and layering (40)”). Adding a sentence linking your alignment mechanism to prior observations of nematic domains in rod-shaped bacteria on surfaces would further situate the work; you already cite 3D nematic order (29).

In sum, this is a compelling and potentially field-shaping study that elevates cell shape—as mediated by emergent nematic alignment—to a dominant determinant of competitive success at colony fronts. Addressing the few confounders (width/volume/mreB pleiotropy; fluorescent-load bias), tightening statistical and image-processing reporting, and adding small robustness tests would substantially strengthen the causal claims without changing scope. My expertise covers bacterial biophysics, active matter modeling, and microbial imaging; I did not assess any code as it was not provided here.
